div.head: On Cattle and Beasts of Burden
div.p: Adam was the first to give names to all living creatures, calling each by a name suited to the present character of the nature it was to serve. The nations, however, gave names to each animal out of their own language. Adam did not impose those names according to the Latin or Greek tongue, or that of any of the barbarian nations, but in that language which, before the Flood, was the one tongue of all -- which is called Hebrew. In Latin, living things are called animalia or animantia because they are quickened by life (anima) and moved by breath (spiritus). They are called quadrupeds because they walk on four feet; such creatures, though similar to cattle, are not under human care -- as stags, does, wild asses, and the rest. Nor are they wild beasts, like lions, nor beasts of burden useful to the service of man. We call "pecus" (livestock) every creature that lacks human speech and shape. The name of livestock properly belongs to those animals fit either for eating, like sheep and pigs, or useful for man's service, like horses and oxen. There is a difference between pecora and pecudes: the ancients used pecora broadly for all animals, but pecudes only for those that are eaten, as though pecuedes. In general every animal is called pecus from pasturing (pascendo). Iumenta (beasts of burden) take their name from the fact that they help (iuvent) our labor by carrying our burdens or by plowing. For the ox draws the cart and turns the hardest clods of earth with the ploughshare; the horse and the donkey carry loads and lighten men's labor in travelling. Hence they are called iumenta, from the fact that they help (iuvant) men, being animals of great strength. They are also called armenta, either because they are fit for arms (armis), that is, for war, or because we use them in arms; others take armenta to mean oxen alone, from ploughing (arando), as though aramenta. There is a distinction between armenta and greges: armenta are of horses and oxen, greges of goats and sheep. The sheep (ovis) is a gentle beast with wool, unarmed in body, peaceful in temper, named from oblatio (offering), because among the ancients it was sheep, not bulls, that were first slaughtered in sacrifice. Some of these are called bidentes, those which among their eight teeth have two that are taller, which the pagans especially offered in sacrifice. The wether (vervex) is named either from vis (strength), because it is stronger than the other sheep, or because it is vir (male), or because it has a worm (vermis) in its head, which, roused by an itch, makes them butt one another and fight violently. The ram (aries) is named either apo tou Areos, that is from Mars, whence among us the males of a flock are called mares -- or because this animal was first sacrificed on the altars (aris) by the pagans. Aries, because it was placed upon the altars (aris). Whence the line: 'A ram is slaughtered at the altar.' The Greeks call the lamb apo tou agnou, as if pious (from hagnos, pure); the Latins think it has this name because, more than other animals, it recognizes (agnoscat) its mother, so much so that even if it has strayed in a large flock, it at once recognizes its parent's voice by her bleating. Kids (haedi) are named from eating (edendo), for they are very fat and of pleasant flavor when young, whence also edulium (food). The he-goat (hircus) is a lustful and wanton animal, always burning for coupling; its eyes look sideways out of lust, whence it takes its name -- for hirqui are, according to Suetonius, the corners of the eyes; its nature is so hot that its blood alone dissolves adamant, a stone that neither fire nor iron can conquer. The larger he-goats are called Cinyphian, from the river Cinyps in Libya, where large ones are born. Some derive capri and caprae (goats) from browsing (carpendis) on bushes; others, because they seek out (captent) rough places. Some derive it from the creaking (crepitu) of their legs, whence they were called crepae; these are the wild goats, which the Greeks, because they see very sharply (oxyderkestaton), called dorkas. They dwell on the highest mountains, and though from far off, they see all who approach. The same applies to roe deer (capreae) and to ibexes, as if avices, because, like birds, they occupy the heights and dwell aloft, so that from that height they are scarcely visible to human sight. Whence the southern peoples call ibexes birds, those who dwell by the streams of the Nile. These animals, as we have said, dwell on the highest crags, and if ever they sense the approach of wild beasts or men, they hurl themselves down from the highest peaks of the rocks and land unharmed upon their own horns. Stags (cervi) are named apo ton keraton, that is from their horns (keras in Greek meaning horn). These are enemies of serpents, and when they feel themselves weighed down by sickness, they draw the serpents out of their lairs with the breath of their nostrils, and having overcome the danger of the venom, are restored by feeding on them. They discovered the herb dittany, for having grazed on it, they shake out any arrows lodged in them. They marvel at the sound of pipes. With ears erect they hear sharply, but nothing when their ears droop. When they swim across vast rivers or seas, they lay their heads upon the haunches of those swimming ahead, and taking turns in succession, feel no burden of weight. The tragelaphi are so named by the Greeks, which, though of the same appearance as stags, have shaggy shoulders like goats, and chins bristling with long beards; they are found nowhere but around the Phasis. Fawns (hinnuli) are the young of stags -- named from 'nodding' (innuere), because they hide themselves at their mother's signal. The doe (dammula) is so named because it slips from the hand (de manu effugiat); it is a timid and unwarlike animal, of which Martial says: 'The boar is feared for its tusk, horns defend the stag; what but prey are we unwarlike does?' The hare (lepus) is called levipes (light-foot), because it runs swiftly; whence in Greek too it is called lagos from its running, for it is a swift and very timid animal. Rabbits (cuniculi) are a kind of wild animal, called as though caniculi, because they are caught or driven from their burrows by the tracking of dogs. The pig (sus) is named because it roots up (subigat) pasture, that is, it turns up the earth in search of food. The boar (verres) is named because it has great strength (vires). The word porcus is as though spurcus (filthy). For it wallows in mud, buries itself in mire, smears itself with slime; Horace says: 'and the sow, friend of mud.' Hence too are named spurcitia (filth) and spurii (bastards). The bristles of pigs we call setae, and setae are named from sus, whence also shoemakers (sutores) are named, because they sew (suunt, i.e. consuant) hides with bristles. The wild boar (aper) is named from its ferocity (feritate), with the letter f changed to p. Whence among the Greeks too it is called suagros, that is, wild; for everything that is wild and untamed we loosely call agreste. The young bullock (iuvencus) is so named because it begins to be of use (iuvare) to men in tilling the soil, or because among the pagans it was always the young bullock, never the full-grown bull, that was sacrificed to Jupiter; for in sacrificial victims the age too was considered. Taurus (bull) is a Greek word, as is bos (ox). Indian bulls are tawny in color, swift as birds, with their hair growing backward; they can turn their heads about with great flexibility; the hardness of their hide repels every weapon, such is their untamed ferocity. The Greeks call the ox 'boun.' The Latins call it trio, as though terio, because it wears down (terat) the earth. Naevius: 'Here the rustic driver of the plough-oxen.' The loose skin hanging from the chin to the legs is called the dewlap (palearia), from pellis (hide), as though pellearia -- a mark of nobility in an ox. Among their fellows, oxen show remarkable affection: each seeks out the one with which it is used to drawing the plough, and testifies its loyal affection with frequent lowing if its partner should happen to be missing. The cow (vacca) is named as though boacca; for it belongs to the class of movable nouns, like leo/leaena (lion/lioness), draco/dracaena (dragon/she-dragon). The calf (vitulus, vitula) is named from viriditas (freshness), that is, from its green age, as with virgo (maiden). A vitula, then, is a young female that has not yet calved; once she has calved, she is a iuvenca or vacca. Buffaloes (bubali) are named by derivation, because they resemble oxen; so untamed are they that out of ferocity they will not accept the yoke on their necks. Africa produces these. Aurochs (uri) are wild oxen found in Germany, having horns stretched out so far that cups of remarkable capacity are made from them for royal tables. They are called uri apo ton oreon, that is, from the mountains. The camel (camelus) gets its name either because, when loaded, it crouches down to become shorter and lower -- for the Greeks call low and short chamai -- or because it is curved in the back, for kamour in Greek signifies curved. Other regions too send these, but Arabia sends the most. They differ among themselves: Arabian camels have two humps on the back, those of other regions have but one. The dromedary is a kind of camel, of smaller stature but swifter -- whence also its name, for dromos in Greek signifies running and speed. It is accustomed to cover a hundred miles or more in a single day. This animal, like the ox and the sheep and the camel, chews the cud (ruminates); rumination is so called from the ruma, a projecting part of the throat, through which the food, once sent down, is called back up again by certain animals. The donkey and its young, the ass, are named from sitting (a sedendo), as though asedus; but this name, which more properly belonged to horses, was taken up by this animal because, before men had tamed horses, it was the ass they first put to use. Being a slow animal and offering no resistance for any reason, man subdued it to himself as soon as he wished. The wild ass (onager) is interpreted as 'wild ass' -- for the Greeks call the donkey onos, and agrion means wild. Africa has these, large and untamed, wandering in the desert. Each herd of females has one male at its head. When males are born, the herd-leaders grow jealous and bite off their testicles, which the mothers, wary of this, guard by hiding them in secret places. Arcadian asses are so called because they were first brought from Arcadia, large and tall. The smaller donkey is more useful on the farm, since it endures labor and hardly refuses any task, however unpleasant. Horses (equi) are so named because, when yoked to a chariot in fours, they were matched (aequabantur), being paired in form and alike in their running. The workhorse (caballus) was earlier called cabo, from the way its striking hoof, as it walks, hollows out the ground -- something the other animals do not do. Hence too it is called sonipes (sound-foot), because it resounds with its feet. Horses show great vitality: they exult in the open fields; they scent battle; they are roused to fight by the sound of the trumpet; excited by a voice, they are spurred to the gallop; they grieve when defeated, and exult when victorious. Some sense their enemies in battle, so much so that they attack their adversaries by biting; some recognize their own masters, forgetting their gentleness if the rider changes; some accept no rider but their own master upon their back; many shed tears when their masters are killed or dying. The horse alone, it is said, weeps for man's sake and feels the emotion of grief. Whence in the Centaurs the natures of horse and man are mingled together. Those about to fight are also accustomed to gather an omen of the outcome from the sadness or eagerness of their horses. The lifespan of horses is long -- Persian, Hunnic, Epirote, and Sicilian horses commonly live beyond fifty years, but it is generally held to be shorter for Spanish, Numidian, and Gallic horses. In noble horses, as the ancients say, four things are looked to: form, beauty, merit, and color. Form: that the body be strong and solid, with a height suited to its strength, a long flank, haunches drawn in tight and rounded, a broad open chest, the whole body knotted with dense muscle, a dry hoof solidified into a concave horn. Beauty: that the head be small and lean, the skin clinging close to the bone, short and sharp ears, large eyes, wide nostrils, an erect neck, thick mane and tail, and hooves of fixed, rounded solidity. Merit: that it be bold in spirit, quick of foot, with trembling limbs -- a sign of vigor -- that it be readily roused from deepest calm, yet, once roused to speed, not too hard to restrain. The horse's alertness is understood from its ears, its vigor from its trembling limbs. Color is especially to be noted: bay, golden, rose-colored, myrtle, deer-colored, dun, grey, dappled, roan, white, spotted, black. In the next rank, one marked with black-and-bay mixture; other mixed colors, or ash-grey, are worst of all. The ancients called bay (badius) vadius, because among the other animals it goes forward (vadat) most boldly. The same is called spadix, which they term phoenicatum, spadix being named from the color of the date-palm, which the Sicilians call spadica. Grey (glaucus) is as though having eyes touched with a certain gleaming brightness -- for the ancients used glaucus in this sense. Dun (gilvus) is a pale yellowish color. Spotted (guttatus) is white with black flecks interspersed. White (candidus) and pale (albus) differ from one another: albus has a certain pallor, while candidus is snow-white and suffused with pure brightness. Grey (canus) is so named because it is made of white and black together. Roan (scutulatus) is named from the white circles it bears amid the dark patches. Dappled (varius) is so named because it has streaks of uneven colors. Those which have only white feet are called petili; those with a white forehead, calidi. The deer-colored (cervinus) is what common speech calls guaranen. The common folk also call it aeranen, because it is of a bronze-like color. Myrtle-colored (myrteus) is a dark shade of purple. It is called dosinus because its color resembles that of the donkey -- the same as ashen. These come from a wild stock, which we call feral horses, and for that reason cannot pass over into the dignity of city use. Mauron is black; for the Greeks call black mauron. The pony (mannus), which common speech calls brunicus, is a smaller horse. The ancients called post-horses veredi, because they drew the redae (carriages), that is, drove them, or because they ran along the public roads, on which the redae were accustomed to travel. There are three kinds of horses: one noble, fit for battle and for burdens; another common and of the herd, fit for drawing but not for riding; a third arising from a mixture of the two different kinds, also called bigenerum because it is born of different stocks, as the mule. The word mulus (mule) is drawn from Greek, because, subdued to the miller's yoke, it drives the millstones round in their slow circling. The Jews assert that Anah, great-grandson of Esau, was the first to mount mares to donkeys in the desert, that from this new animals contrary to nature -- mules -- might be born. Wild asses too were admitted to she-asses for this purpose, and he is said to have discovered such a mating so that the swiftest of donkeys might be born from it. Human ingenuity, indeed, forced different animals to mate, and by this adulterous mixture discovered another kind -- just as Jacob too, contrary to nature, procured similarities of color. For his ewes conceived offspring of such a kind as they had beheld in the reflections in the water, the shadows of the rams mounting above them. It is said, too, that this same thing happens among herds of mares, that noble stallions are placed before the sight of the conceiving females, so that they may conceive and produce offspring like them. And so lovers of doves place painted images of the most beautiful doves in the very places where the doves dwell, so that, their sight being captivated, they may breed similar offspring. Hence it is that some order pregnant women not to look upon the ugliest of animals' faces, such as dog-headed apes and monkeys, lest, coming upon their sight, they bear offspring resembling them. For it is said to be the nature of women that whatever they have gazed upon, or conceived in the mind, at the utmost height of pleasure, while they conceive, they bring forth offspring of that same kind. For indeed the animal, in the act of Venus, transmits inward the forms it receives from without, and, its imagination sated by their images, seizes their likeness into its own nature. Among living creatures those are called bigenera which are born of different kinds, as the mule from a mare and a donkey; the hinny (burdo) from a horse and a she-ass; hybrids from wild boars and domestic pigs; the tityrus from a sheep and a he-goat; the musmo from a she-goat and a ram. It is the leader of the flock.

div.head: On Wild Beasts
div.p: The word 'beasts' (bestiae) properly applies to lions, leopards, tigers, wolves, and foxes and dogs and apes and the rest, which rage either with mouth or with claws -- serpents excepted. They are called bestiae from the vis (force) with which they rage. They are called ferae because they follow their natural freedom and are borne along by their own desire; for their wills are free, and they wander here and there, borne wherever their spirit leads them. The word 'lion' (leo) is a Greek word bent into Latin form; for in Greek it is called leon, and it is a bastard word, being in part corrupted. Leaena (lioness), however, is wholly Greek, as is dracaena (she-dragon). That leaena is said as lea is a usage taken up by the poets. Leo, in Greek, is interpreted in Latin as 'king,' because he is the chief of all beasts. His kind is said to be threefold. Of these, the short-maned with curly mane are unwarlike; the long-maned with straight hair are fierce. Their spirit is shown by the brow and the tail. Their strength is in the chest, their firmness in the head. When hemmed in by hunters they fix their gaze on the ground, so as to be less terrified by the sight of the hunting-spears. They fear the creaking of wheels, but fire more. When they sleep, their eyes keep watch; when they walk, they cover their own tracks with their tail, lest the hunter find them. When they have begotten a cub, the cub is said to sleep for three days and three nights; then, as if roused by the growling or roaring of its father, the sleeping place is said to be shaken and the sleeping cub is roused. Toward man, it is the nature of lions that they cannot grow angry unless they are injured. Their mercy is evident in constant examples: they spare those laid prostrate; they let captives who cross their path go free; they kill a man only in great hunger. Of these Lucretius speaks: 'and the whelps of lions.' The tiger (tigris) is named from its swift flight, for so the Persians and Medes name an arrow. It is a beast marked with varied spots, remarkable for strength and speed; from its name the river Tigris takes its name, because it is the swiftest of all rivers. Hyrcania chiefly breeds these. The panther (panther) is named either because it is friendly to every animal except the dragon, or because it delights in the company of its own kind and returns in the same fashion whatever it receives. For pan in Greek means 'all.' It is a beast painted over with small round spots, so marked with tawny eye-like rings that it is distinguished by dark or white variety. This creature gives birth entirely only once; the reason for this is clear. For when the cubs have grown together in the mother's womb and, with mature strength, are ready to be born, they hate the delay of time; and so, the womb being burdened with the young as though hindering the birth, they tear it with their claws: she casts out, or rather releases, her offspring, forced by the pain. Afterward, the birth-passages being torn and scarred, the seed of generation, once received, does not hold, but leaps back in vain. For Pliny says that animals furnished with sharp claws are unable to give birth often, since they are injured internally by the movement of their own cubs. The leopard (pardus) ranks second after the panther, a spotted and very swift kind, headlong toward bloodshed; for it rushes upon its prey with a leap even unto death. The 'leopardus' is born of the adulterous union of a lioness and a leopard, and produces a third stock -- just as Pliny too says in his Natural History, that a lion mates with a female leopard, or a leopard with a lioness, and from either union degenerate offspring are created, like the mule and the hinny. The rhinoceros is so named by the Greeks; in Latin it is interpreted 'horn on the nose.' The same is also called monoceros, that is, unicorn, because it has a single horn in the middle of its forehead, four feet long, so sharp and strong that whatever it strikes it either tosses aside or pierces through. For it often does battle even with elephants, and lays them low, wounded in the belly. It is said to be of such great strength that it cannot be caught by any hunter's skill; but, as those who have written on the natures of animals assert, a virgin girl is set before it, who, as it approaches, opens her lap, in which the beast, laying aside all its fierceness, lays down its head, and so, lulled to sleep, is captured as though unarmed. The Greeks think the elephant (elephas) is named from the size of its body, because it displays the form of a mountain -- for a mountain in Greek is called lophos. Among the Indians, however, it is named from its cry, barrus; whence too its trumpeting is called barritus, and its tusks ebur (ivory). Its snout is called the proboscis, because with it the animal brings food to its mouth; and it is like a serpent, defended by a rampart of ivory. The Romans of old called these creatures Lucan oxen -- 'oxen' because they saw no animal of greater size, 'Lucan' because Pyrrhus first threw them against the Romans in battle in Lucania. This kind of creature is indeed useful in warfare; for the Persians and Indians, with wooden towers placed upon them, fight with javelins as though from a wall. They abound also in intelligence and memory. They walk in herds; they greet one another with the motion in which their strength lies; they flee from the mouse; they mate facing away from each other; and when they give birth, they release their young in waters or on islands, on account of dragons, which are their enemies and are killed by being entangled by them. They carry their young for two years, and give birth no more than once, and no more than one at a time; they live three hundred years. Formerly elephants were born only in Africa and India; now India alone produces them. The griffin (gryps) is so called because it is a winged and four-footed creature. This kind of beast is born in the Hyperborean mountains. In every part of its body it is a lion; in wings and face it resembles an eagle; it is fiercely hostile to horses. Indeed it tears apart any men it sees. The chameleon does not have one color, but is marked with varied hues, like the leopard, and is so named for this reason. The little body of this chameleon changes very readily to whatever colors it sees, a facility of change not found in the bodily substance of other animals. The giraffe (camelopardus) is so named because, while spotted with white patches like the leopard, it has a neck like a horse, feet like an ox, yet a head like a camel. Ethiopia produces this creature. The lynx is so named because it is counted in the wolf family; a beast marked on the back with spots like the leopard, but resembling a wolf -- whence the Greek lykos (wolf) gives lynx its name. Its urine, they say, turns into the hardness of a precious stone called lyncurium, which the lynxes themselves are proven to sense by this fact: they cover their voided liquid with sand as far as they are able, out of a certain jealousy of nature, lest such excretion pass into human use. Pliny the Elder says that lynxes never bear more than one cub at a time. Beavers (castores) are named from castrando (castrating). For their testicles are useful for medicines, on account of which, when pursued...

div.head: On the Smaller Creatures
div.p: The mouse (mus) is a tiny animal. Its name is Greek; whatever is derived from it becomes Latin. Others say mice are called mures because they are born from the moisture (humor) of the earth; for mus comes from terra (earth), whence also humus. At the full moon their liver grows, just as certain sea creatures increase, and then diminish again as the moon wanes. Sorex (shrew) is Latin, because it gnaws (rodat) and cuts things through in the manner of a saw (serra). The ancients called the shrew soricem instead of sauricem, just as they said clodus for claudus (lame). The weasel (mustela) is so named as though mus longus (long mouse); for telum is derived from length. This creature, cunning by nature, moves and changes its lair in the houses where it raises its young. It also hunts serpents and mice. There are two kinds of weasel: one is wild and lives in the woods, of greater size, which the Greeks call iktidas; the other wanders about in houses. Those are mistaken who say that the weasel conceives through the mouth and gives birth through the ear. The shrew-mouse (mus araneus), by whose bite comes the spider's poison. There is in Sardinia a very tiny creature, in the shape of a spider, which is called the solifuga, because it flees the light. It is very common in silver mines, creeping about unseen, and through carelessness brings death to those who sit upon it. The mole (talpa) is so named because it is condemned to perpetual blindness in darkness. For it has no eyes, it always digs the earth, throws up the soil, and eats the roots beneath the crops; the Greeks call it asphalax. Dormice (glires) are so called because sleep makes them fat; for we say gliscere for 'to grow.' For the whole of winter they sleep and lie motionless as though dead, and in the summer season they come back to life. The hedgehog (ericius) is an animal covered with spines, named for this reason, because it curls itself up whenever it is enclosed by its own spines, by which it is protected on every side against ambush. For as soon as it senses anything, it first curls itself up, and, rolled into a ball, gathers itself back into its own weapons. It has a certain cleverness: when it has cut a grape-cluster from the vine, it rolls onto its back over it, and so carries it to its young. The cricket (gryllus) takes its name from the sound of its voice. It walks backward, bores into the earth, and chirps by night. It is hunted by tying an ant with a hair and dropping it into its burrow, dust having first been blown in so that it cannot hide; thus it is drawn out by the ant's grip. The ant (formica) is so named because it carries (ferat) crumbs (micas) of grain. Its cleverness is great: it looks ahead to the future, and in summer prepares what it will eat in winter; at harvest it chooses wheat, and does not touch barley; when rain falls on its grain, it throws the whole lot out. It is said that in Ethiopia there are ants in the shape of dogs, which dig golden sand with their feet, and guard it so that none may carry it off, pursuing to the death those who try to seize it. The ant-lion (formicoleon) is so called because it is, as it were, the lion of the ants, or rather at once ant and lion. For it is a small creature very hostile to ants, which hides itself in the dust and kills ants carrying grain. It is therefore called both lion and ant, because to other animals it is as an ant, but to ants it is as a lion.

div.head: On Serpents
div.p: The word 'snake' (anguis) is the general name for every serpent that can be coiled and twisted; and it is called anguis because it is angular (angulosus) and never straight. Among the pagans, snakes were always regarded as the spirits of places, whence Persius: 'paint two snakes: boys, this is a sacred place.' The grass-snake (coluber) is so named either because it inhabits (colat) the shade, or because it glides along in slippery, sinuous windings. For anything is called lubricum (slippery) that slips while being held, as a fish or a serpent. The serpent (serpens) takes its name because it creeps (serpit) by hidden approach, not by open steps, but crawls by the tiniest efforts of its scales. Those creatures which rest on four feet, like lizards and geckos, are called not serpents but reptiles. Serpents, however, are also reptiles, because they crawl on belly and breast. They have as many venoms as kinds, as many forms of death as species, as many pains as colors. The dragon (draco) is the largest of all serpents, indeed of all living creatures on earth. The Greeks call it drakon, whence the Latin draco is derived. It is often said to be drawn out from caves into the air, and the air is stirred by its passing. It has a crest, a small mouth, and narrow pipes through which it draws breath and puts out its tongue. Its power lies not in its teeth but in its tail, and it does harm by lashing rather than by biting. It is harmless as regards venom, since it needs no poison to bring death, for if it wraps itself around anyone, it kills. Not even the elephant is safe from it because of its bodily size; for lurking near the paths along which elephants are accustomed to walk, it binds their legs in coils and suffocates and destroys them. It is born in Ethiopia and India, in the very furnace of continual heat. The basilisk, in Greek, is interpreted in Latin as regulus (little king), because it is king of the serpents, so much so that those who see it flee, since it kills by its very smell; indeed it kills a man even by its gaze. Not even a bird flying past its sight passes unharmed, but however far off it may be, it is burned up in its mouth and devoured. Yet it is overcome by weasels, which men bring into the caverns where it lurks; and so, at the sight of it, the weasel gives chase and kills it, fleeing though it be. For the Author of all things established nothing without a remedy. It is about half a foot in length, marked with white spots. The basilisks, like scorpions, seek out dry places, and once they have come to water, cause hydrophobia and madness in those who drink. The 'sibilus' is the same as the basilisk. For it kills with a hiss, before it bites or burns. The viper (vipera) is named because it gives birth by force (vi pariat). For when its womb groans in labor, the young, not waiting for the natural time of birth, burst forth by force, gnawing through the mother's sides, and she dies in the process. Lucan: 'the viper's knots come together, its body torn open.' It is said that the male inserts his mouth and spits his seed into the viper; she, turned to rage by the pleasure of lust, bites off the male's head, taken into her mouth. Thus it happens that both parents perish: the male in mating, the female in giving birth. From the viper are made lozenges which the Greeks call theriaka. The asp (aspis) is so named because by its bite it sends forth and scatters venom; for the Greeks call venom ios, whence aspis, because it kills by its venomous bite. There are various kinds and species of it, and unequal effects in doing harm. It is said that the asp, when it begins to suffer from a snake-charmer who calls it out of its cave with certain incantations of his own, if it does not wish to come out, presses one ear to the ground and covers the other with its tail, and so, not hearing those magic words, does not come out to the charmer. The dipsas, a kind of asp, is called in Latin situla, because whoever it bites dies of thirst. The hypnalis, a kind of asp, is so named because it kills by sleep. Cleopatra applied this to herself, and so was released by a death like sleep. The haemorrhois asp is named because it makes whoever it has bitten sweat blood, so that, the veins dissolved, whatever life remains is drawn out through the blood -- for blood in Greek is haima. The prester asp always runs with its mouth open and steaming. The poet remembers it thus: 'and the greedy prester stretching its smoking jaws.' Whoever it strikes swells up and dies from an enormous bloating; for putrefaction follows the swelling. The seps, a wasting asp, when it has bitten a man, at once consumes him, so that he entirely dissolves in the serpent's mouth. The horned viper (cerastes) is so named because it has horns on its head like a ram's -- for the Greeks call horns kerata; it has four small horns, by the display of which, as by bait, it lures and destroys animals enticed by curiosity. It covers its whole body with sand, giving no sign of itself except in that part by which it catches the birds or animals it has enticed. It is more flexible than other serpents, so much so that it seems to have no spine. The scytale serpent is so named because it gleams with such variety on its back that it delays onlookers in wonder at its markings; and because it is rather slow in crawling, it catches those it cannot pursue by the wonder of its appearance, which leaves them dazed. Its heat is so great that even in wintertime it sheds the skin of its still-burning body. Of this Lucan says: 'and the scytale, alone still shedding its skin amid the scattered frosts.' The amphisbaena is so named because it has two heads, one in its own place, the other in its tail, running from either head, its body moving in a circle. This alone of serpents endures cold, being the first of all to come forth. Of this the same Lucan says: 'and the amphisbaena, heavy, bending toward its twin head.' Its eyes shine like lamps. The enhydris is a water-snake living in water; for the Greeks call water hydor. The hydros is a water-serpent, by whose strike those bitten swell up; some call the resulting illness boa, because it is treated with cow dung. The hydra is a many-headed dragon, such as was in the Lernaean marsh in the province of Arcadia. This is called in Latin excetra, because when one head was cut off, three grew back. But this is a fable; for it is known that the Hydra was a place spewing forth waters that laid waste the neighboring city, in which, when one channel was closed, many others burst forth; seeing this, Hercules burned the very ground and so closed the channels of the water. For Hydra is named from hydor, water. The chelydros serpent, also called chersydros, as if from 'cheris,' because it dwells both in waters and on land; for the Greeks call land cherson, water hydor. Wherever it glides, it makes the earth smoke; of which Macer thus writes: 'whether its foaming back breathes forth poison, or the earth smokes where the foul serpent glides.' And Lucan: 'and the chelydrus dragging its smoking track.' It always moves in a straight line; for if it twists itself while running, it at once bursts. The natrix is a serpent that poisons water; whatever spring it enters, it infects with venom. Of which Lucan: 'the natrix, defiler of the water.' The cenchris serpent is not sinuous, always making a straight path; of which Lucan: 'and the cenchris, ever gliding on a straight track.' The parias is a serpent that always moves upon its tail and seems to make a furrow; of which the same poet: 'content to furrow its path with its tail, the parias.' The boa, an Italian serpent of immense bulk, pursues herds of cattle and buffalo, and, twining itself about the swollen udders, kills by sucking milk -- and from this depopulation of cattle (boves) it takes the name boa. The iaculus is a flying serpent; of which Lucan: 'and the flying spears (iaculi).' They leap out from trees, and whenever some animal comes their way, they hurl themselves upon it and kill it; whence they are called iaculi (javelins). In Arabia there are winged serpents called sirens, which run faster than horses, and are even said to fly; their venom is so potent that death follows the bite before the pain does. The ophites is so named because it has the color of sand; of which the poet says: 'the Theban ophites, marked with such tiny spots, matching the burnt sands and indistinguishable from them.' The seps is a tiny serpent that consumes not only the flesh but the very bones with its venom; of which the poet thus writes: 'and the wasting seps, dissolving both bone and body.' The dipsas serpent is said to be of such tininess that when trodden upon, it is not seen. Its venom kills before it is felt, so that the face of the dying, its death anticipated, takes on no look of sorrow. Of which the poet says: 'the standard-bearer, a youth of Tyrrhenian blood, Aulus, was struck by the dipsas trodden underfoot, its head twisted back: scarcely was there pain or any sense of the bite.' The salpuga is a serpent that is not seen. The caecula is so named because it is small and has no eyes. The centipede is named from its multitude of feet. The lizard (lacertus) is a kind of reptile, named because it has 'arms' (brachia). There are several kinds of lizards: the toad-lizard, the salamander, the skink, and the gecko (stellio). The botrax is so named because it has a face like a frog's -- for the Greeks call the frog batrachos. The salamander is so named because it has power against fires. Among all venomous creatures its power is the greatest; for the others harm one at a time, but this one kills many at once. For if it creeps onto a tree, it poisons all the fruit, and kills those who eat it; even if it falls into a well, the force of its venom kills those who drink from it. Resisting fire, it alone among animals extinguishes flames; for it lives amid the flames without pain or being consumed, and not only is it not burned, but it puts out the fire. The skink lizard, when it grows old, has its eyes blinded, and it enters a hole in a wall facing east, and as the sun rises it gazes at it and is illuminated. The gecko (stellio) has its name given from its color; for it is marked on its back with shining spots like stars. Of which Ovid says: 'and it has a name fitting its color, its body starred with varied spots.' This creature is said to be so hostile to scorpions that the sight of it brings them fear and paralysis. There are other kinds of serpents: the ammodytae, the elephantiae, the chamaedracontes. In sum, as many as their names, so many are their kinds of death...

div.head: On Worms
div.p: A worm (vermis) is an animal that is generally born from flesh, or from wood, or from any earthly matter whatsoever, without any mating; though sometimes they are also born from eggs, as the scorpion. Worms belong either to earth, water, air, flesh, foliage, wood, or clothing. The spider (aranea) is a worm of the air, named from its nourishment by the air; with its tiny body it draws out long threads, and, ever intent upon its web, never ceases its labor, sustaining an endless hanging-toil in its craft. The leech (sanguisuga) is an aquatic worm, so named because it sucks blood. It lies in wait for those who drink; and when it slips down the throat, or attaches wherever it can, it drains the blood; and when it has grown heavy with too much blood, it vomits up what it has drawn, so as to suck fresh blood again. The scorpion is an earthly worm, more properly assigned to the worms than to the serpents; an animal armed with a sting, and named in Greek from the fact that it strikes with its tail and spreads its venom through an arching wound. It is a peculiarity of the scorpion that it does not strike the palm of the hand. The blister-beetle (cantharis) is an earthly worm which, once applied to the human body, raises blisters full of fluid by its burning. The millipede is an earthly worm, named from its multitude of feet, which curls into a ball when touched. It is born beneath rocks, from moisture and earth. The slug (limax) is a worm of mud (limus), so named because it is born in mud or from mud; whence it is always held to be filthy and unclean. The silkworm (bombyx) is a worm of leaves, from whose weaving silk (bombycinum) is made. It is given this name because it empties itself out as it spins its threads, so that only air remains within it. The caterpillar (eruca) is a leaf-worm found on cabbage, or wrapped in a vine-leaf, named from erodendo (gnawing away). Of which Plautus makes mention: 'like a worthless and harmful creature, wrapped in a vine-leaf, it enfolds itself.' Unlike the locust, it does not fly off here and there leaving crops half-eaten, but remains, and with slow movement and sluggish bites consumes the whole of the crops that are about to perish. The Greeks call wood-worms teredones, because they gnaw through (terendo) wood. We call these termites. For so, among the Latins, the worms of wood are named, which trees felled at an untimely season produce. The moth (tinea) is a worm of clothing, named because it holds fast (teneat) and settles in so as to gnaw through. Hence too pertinax (persistent), because it presses again and again at the same thing. Worms of the flesh: the head-worm, the tapeworm, roundworms, intestinal worms, lice, fleas, nits, the lard-worm, the ear-mite, the hog-louse, the bedbug. The hemicranius is the worm named for the head. The tapeworm (lumbricus) is an intestinal worm, named as though lumbicus, because it slips (labitur), or because it is in the loins (lumbis). Roundworms. Intestinal worms. Lice (peduculi) are skin-worms named from the feet (pedibus); whence too the lice-ridden (peducosi) are those in whose bodies lice swarm. Fleas (pulices) are so named because they feed chiefly on dust (pulvis). Nits. The lard-worm (tarmus) is the worm of lard. The ear-mite (ricinus) is the worm of the dog, so named because it clings in the ears of dogs -- for kyon in Greek means dog. The hog-louse (usia) is the worm of the pig, so named because it burns (urit); for wherever it bites, the place burns so much that blisters form there. The bedbug (cimex) is named from its likeness to a certain herb, whose stench it shares. Properly, the vermis is born in decaying flesh; the tinea in clothing; the eruca in vegetables; the teredo in wood; the tarmus in lard. The worm does not creep like the serpent, with open steps or by the effort of its scales, because it has no rigid spine, like the grass-snake; but by stretching forward, part by part, the contracted portions of its little body, and then contracting the extended parts, it works out its motion, and thus, agitated, glides along.

div.head: On Fish
div.p: Fish (pisces) are so named, whence also pecus (livestock), from pasturing (pascendo). They are called reptiles because, though they swim, they have the appearance and nature of creeping (reptandi); for even though they plunge into the deep, they still 'creep' as they swim. Whence David says: 'This sea, great and wide, wherein are creeping things innumerable.' Some kinds of fish are amphibious, so called because they have both the habit of walking on land and the office of swimming in the waters. For amphi in Greek signifies 'both,' that is, because they live both in the waters and on land -- as seals, crocodiles, and hippopotami, that is, river-horses. Now men gave names to livestock and wild beasts and birds before they did to fish, because these were seen and known first. The names of fish, however, were established gradually as their kinds became known, either from a resemblance to land creatures, or from their own particular appearance or habits, or color, or shape, or sex. From resemblance to land creatures: as the sea-frog, the sea-calf, sea-lions, black sea-blackbirds, and sea-peacocks of varied colors, marked on back and neck, and sea-thrushes speckled with white, and the rest which have claimed for themselves names drawn from the appearance of land animals. From the habits of land animals: as sea-dogs, named from land dogs because they bite; and sea-wolves, because with shameless voracity they pursue others. From color: as umbrae (shade-fish), because they are the color of shade; and gilt-heads (auratae), because they have a gold color on the head; and 'varii,' from their variegation, commonly called trout. From shape: as the sunfish (orbis), because it is round and consists entirely of its head; as the sole (solea), because it is shaped like the sole of a shoe. From sex: as the mussel (musculus), because it is the male of the whale; for by its mating this creature is said to conceive. Hence too the 'muscles' of snails, by whose milk oysters are said to conceive. Whales (ballenae) are creatures of immense size, named from emitting and pouring forth waters; for beyond other sea creatures they throw their spouts higher -- for ballein in Greek means 'to emit.' The cete are called to ketos kai ta kete, that is, because of their monstrous size. For they are huge kinds of monsters, with bodies equal to mountains -- such was the whale that swallowed Jonah, whose belly was of such magnitude that it held the likeness of hell itself, as the Prophet says: 'He heard me out of the belly of hell.' Sea-horses (equi marini) are so called because their front part is that of a horse, while their hind part dissolves into that of a fish. They call sea-oxen bocas, as though boacas. Sea-blue creatures (caerulei) are named from their color; for caeruleum is green mixed with black, as is the sea. Dolphins have a fixed name, because they follow the voices of men, or because they gather in schools to the sound of music. Nothing in the sea is swifter than these; for often, leaping, they fly right over ships. When they play in the waves and strike the mass of the surging waters with a headlong leap, they seem to signify coming storms. These are properly called 'simones.' There is also a kind of dolphin in the Nile with a serrated back, which kills crocodiles by cutting the tender part of their bellies. Sea-pigs, commonly called suilli, because, while seeking food, they root up the ground beneath the water like a pig, in the manner of swine; for they have the use of their mouths about their throat, and unless they bury their snouts in the sand, they gather no food. Sea-crows are named from the raven-like sound of their voice, because they grunt from the chest, and, betrayed by their own voice, are caught. Tunny (thynni) have a Greek name. These enter in springtime, coming in on the right side, going out on the left. This is thought to be because they see more sharply with their right eyes than with their left. The swordfish (gladius) is so named because it has a pointed snout like a sword; hence it sinks ships by piercing them through. The sawfish (serra) is so named because it has a serrated crest, and swims beneath ships, cutting them. The scorpion-fish is so named because it hurts when picked up by hand. It is said that if ten crabs are bound together with a bundle of basil, all the scorpion-fish in that place will gather there. The weever (aranea, i.e. 'spider-fish') is a kind of fish, so named because it strikes the ear; for it has stings with which it strikes. The crocodile is named from its saffron (croceus) color; it is born in the Nile, a four-footed animal strong both on land and in the water, generally twenty cubits long, armed with the huge size of its teeth and claws, and with skin so hard that it repels the blows of even strong men's stones off its back. By night it rests in the water, by day on land. It hatches its eggs on land; male and female take turns guarding them. Some fish with a serrated crest kill this creature by cutting the tender part of its belly. It alone among animals is said to move its upper jaw. The hippopotamus is so called because it resembles a horse in its back, mane, and neighing, though its snout is turned up, its teeth like a boar's, its tail twisted. By day it stays in the water, by night it grazes the crops; the Nile produces this creature. The pagrus, which the Greeks call phagron because it has hard teeth, so much so that it feeds on oysters in the sea. The dentex is named for the multitude and size of its teeth. The 'hare-fish' (lepus) is named from a resemblance of its head. The wolf-fish (lupus), as has been said, is named for its voracity, a fish clever at avoiding capture: indeed it is said that, surrounded by a net, it ploughs the sand with its tail and, thus buried, passes through the net. The mullet (mullus) is so named because it is soft (mollis) and very tender. It is said that eating it curbs lust but dulls the eyesight; men who are often fed on this fish are said to smell of fish themselves. If a mullet is drowned in wine, those who drink from that wine afterward develop a distaste for wine. The grey mullet (mugilis) has its name because it is very agile (multum agilis). For when it senses the fishermen's traps set for it, it turns back at once and leaps over the net so that you would think the fish was flying. The melanurus is so named because it has a black tail, black fins, and black lines on its body -- for the Greeks call black melan. The 'glaucus' is named from its color, because it is white -- for the Greeks call white glaukon. This fish rarely appears in summer, except when the sky is overcast. The thymallus takes its name from a flower; for thyme is called a flower: for although pleasant in appearance and delightful in taste, it nonetheless, like a flower, gives off a fragrance and breathes forth scents from its body. The parrotfish (escarus) is so named because it alone is said to chew the cud like other ruminants; indeed, other fish do not ruminate. It is said to be clever: caught inside a fish-trap, it does not try to break out headfirst, nor does it thrust its head into the hostile wickerwork, but turning away, it loosens the opening with repeated strikes of its tail, and so returns backward out of it; and if by chance another parrotfish outside sees this struggle, it seizes the tail in its teeth and helps in the effort to break free. The sparus takes its name from the throwing-spear, because it is of the same shape; for land creatures were discovered before sea creatures. For the sparus is a rustic throwing-weapon, named from spargendo (scattering).

The sea-swallow (hirundo, austral fish) is so named either because it takes in the swell of the waters with its mouth, or because this fish appears at the time when the Pleiades begin to set. The saxatile hamio is marked along both sides with unbroken red stripes and other colored ones; it is called hamio because it can only be caught with a hook (hamo). The remora (echenais), a tiny fish half a foot long, took its name because it holds ships fast by clinging to them. However much the winds rush and the storms rage, the ship, as though rooted, seems to stand fast in the sea and not move -- not by holding it back, but merely by clinging to it. The Latins called this creature mora (delay), because it forces ships to stand still. The uranoscopus is named from the eye it has on its head, with which it always gazes upward. The flying-fish (millago) is named because it flies up over the water. Whenever it is seen flying above the water, storms are said to be changing. The dogfish (squatus) is so named because it is rough with scales; from its skin, indeed, wood is polished. The city of Syria now called Tyre was once called Sarra, from a certain fish abundant there which in their own tongue they call 'sar'; from this, fish of similar likeness are called sardae and sardines. Allec is a small fish suited for a salted liquid, whence its name. The aphorus is a small fish which, because of its tininess, cannot be caught with a hook. The eel (anguilla) is named for its resemblance to a snake (anguis). It originates from mud; hence, when caught, it is so slippery that the harder you press it, the faster it slips away. It is said that the Ganges, a river of the East, produces eels thirty feet long. If eels are drowned in wine, those who drink from it afterward develop a distaste for wine. The sea-dragon has spines on its gills pointing toward its tail, which, wherever it strikes, pour forth venom -- whence its name. The moray eel the Greeks call muraina, because it coils itself into circles. It is said to be entirely female, and to conceive by a serpent; for this reason fishermen call it out with a hiss, as though it were a serpent, and so catch it. It is killed with difficulty by a blow of a stick, but at once by a rod. Its life, it is certain, lies in its tail; for when struck on the head, it is scarcely killed, but when struck on the tail, it dies at once. The conger eel. The octopus (polypus), that is 'many-foot,' for it has very many coils. This clever creature, when it seizes a hook, wraps it in its arms, not biting it, nor releasing it until it has gnawed all around the bait. The torpedo-fish is so named because it makes the body grow numb (torpescere) if anyone touches it while it is alive. Pliny relates: 'From the Indian sea, the torpedo, even from far off and at a distance, if touched only by a spear or a rod, numbs even the strongest arms, however swift for running, it binds the legs.' Such is its power that it affects the limbs even by the very air surrounding its body. The cuttlefish (sepia) is so named because it is more easily caught when enclosed by hedges (sepibus); its manner of mating is indecent, for it conceives through the mouth, like the viper. Its ink is said to have such power that, when added to a lamp, some report that Ethiopians appear to be seen once the earlier light is removed. The squid (lulligo). It is said that in the ocean off Mauretania, not far from the river Lixus, so great a multitude of squid fly up out of the water that they can even sink ships. Shellfish and snails (conchae, cochleae) are so named for this reason, that they grow hollow, that is, are emptied, as the moon wanes. For the flesh of all closed sea creatures and shellfish swells with the waxing of the moon, and is emptied with its waning. For when the moon is waxing, it increases moisture; when it is waning, moisture is diminished -- so say the natural philosophers. Conchae is the name in its primary form, cochleae by diminution, as though 'conchleae.' There are many kinds of shellfish; among them the pearl-bearing kind, called 'oceloe,' in whose flesh a precious stone is formed. Those who have written on the nature of living things report that, because at night they open toward the shore and conceive a pearl from the heavenly dew, they are named 'oceloe' for this reason. The murex is a sea-snail, named from its sharpness and roughness, otherwise called conchylium, because when cut open with iron it releases tears of purple color, from which purple dye is made -- whence it is called ostrum, because this dye is drawn from the moisture within the shell. Crabs (cancri) are so named because they are shellfish having legs -- creatures hostile to oysters. They live off their flesh by a remarkable cunning; for since the oyster's hard shell cannot be pried open, the crab watches for when the oyster opens the barrier of its shell, and then secretly throws in a small stone, and, the closing thus obstructed, gnaws away the oyster's flesh. Some report that if ten crabs are tied with a bundle of basil, all the scorpion-fish in that place will gather to it. There are two kinds of crabs: river and sea. The oyster (ostrea) is named from its shell (testa), by which the softness of the flesh within is protected -- for the Greeks call the shell ostra. Ostrea is neuter, though its flesh is called feminine. Mussels (musculi) are, as we said before, the snails from whose 'milk' oysters conceive; and they are called musculi as though masculi (males). Pelorides are named from the promontory of Pelorus in Sicily, where they abound: 'Behold, from the narrow seat of Pelorus, Boreas...' Ungues (razor-clams) are named from their resemblance to human fingernails (unguium). The tortoise (testudo) is so named because it is covered over with the covering of a shell (testa), in the manner of a vaulted chamber. There are four kinds: land, sea, mud-dwellers (that is, living in mire and marshes), and a fourth kind, river tortoises, which live in fresh water. Some report, incredible as it seems, that ships carrying a tortoise's right foot travel more slowly. The sea-urchin (echinus) takes its name from the land hedgehog, which common speech calls the hedgehog (iricium); its shell is double, spined like little chestnuts when they still fall covered from the trees. Its flesh is soft and reddish. 'Uris' is used in three senses: of the tortoise, of the pelorides, and of the snail. For both what we eat and the place where the flesh is, are called pelorides. Frogs (ranae) are named from their croaking (garrulitas), because they make noise around marshes at breeding time, and give back sounds of their voice with tiresome cries. Of these, some are called water-frogs, some marsh-frogs, some 'rubetae,' because they live among brambles, the largest of all. Others are called reed-frogs, because they live among reeds and bushes, the smallest of all and greenest; mute and voiceless. Little field-frogs (agredulae) dwell in dry places or in fields; hence their name. Some say that dogs will not bark if given a live frog in a piece of meat. The sponge (sfungia) is named from 'shaping,' that is, cleaning and wiping; Afranius: 'I approach you, to wipe your neck with a linen cloth' -- that is, to clean it. Cicero: 'the blood was wiped away with sponges,' that is, cleaned off. It is taught to be an animal, from the blood clinging to the rocks; whence, when it is cut, it releases blood. For some creatures live in the water and move about, like fish; others remain fixed in place, like oysters, sea-urchins, sponges. Of these, some are called male, because their pores are narrow and thicker-walled; others female...

div.head: On Birds
div.p: 'Bird' (avis) is one name, but the kinds are many. For as they differ from one another in appearance, so too in the diversity of their nature. Some are simple, like doves; some are cunning, like the partridge; some submit themselves to the hand, like the hawk; some shy away, like the garamantes; some delight in the company of men, like the swallow; some love a hidden life in the wilderness, like the turtledove; some feed only on seeds they find, like the goose; others eat flesh and are given to plunder, like the kite; some are native, remaining always in the same place, like the ostrich; others are migratory, returning at their own proper seasons, like storks and swallows; some flock together, that is, fly in a group, like starlings and quails; some are solitary, that is, alone, for the sake of preying by ambush, like the eagle, the hawk, and creatures of that kind; some are noisy in their cries, like the swallow; some produce the sweetest songs, like the swan and the blackbird; some imitate the words and voices of men, like the parrot and the magpie. But just as their kinds are countless, so too their habits are innumerable; for no one can discover how many kinds of birds there are. No one has been able to penetrate the whole of the wilds of India, Ethiopia, or Scythia, to know their kinds or differences. Birds (aves) are so named because they do not have fixed roads (viae), but run about through pathless places (avia) wherever they will. Alites are so named because they lift themselves up on high with their wings (alis), and rise to the heights by the rowing of their wings. Volucres (flying things) are named from flying (volando); for whence we say 'to fly' we also say 'to walk' -- for vola is the name for the middle part of the foot or the hand, and in birds the vola is the middle part of the wings, whose movement stirs the feathers; hence volucres. The young of all birds are called 'pulli'; but the young of four-footed animals too are called pulli, and even a small child is called a pullus. Newly born young are called pulli because they are 'polluted' (polluti); whence too black clothing is called pulla. Wings (alae) are those parts in which the feathers, fixed in rows, serve the use of flight. They are called alae because with them the birds nourish (alant) and cherish their embraced young. The feather (pinna) is named from 'hanging' (pendendo), that is, from flying; whence too pendere (to hang). For birds are moved by the aid of their feathers when they commit themselves to the air. Down (pluma) is as though piluma; for as hairs are on the body of four-footed creatures, so down is on birds. Many names of birds are agreed to be formed from the sound of their cry: as the crane, the raven, the swan, the peacock, the kite, the screech-owl, the cuckoo, the jackdaw, and the rest. For the variety of their cries taught men what to call them. The eagle (aquila) is named from the sharpness (acumen) of its eyes. It is said to have such keen sight that when it is borne with motionless wing above the sea, invisible to human eyes, from such a height it can see little fish swimming, and, descending like a thunderbolt, drags its seized prey to the shore with its wings. It is also said not to turn its gaze even against the rays of the sun; whence it holds up its young, suspended by its talons, to the sun's rays, and preserves as worthy of its stock those it sees keep their gaze unmoving, but casts away as unworthy any it sees turn their eyes away. The vulture (vultur) is thought to be named from its slow flight (volatu tardo); for despite the size of its body, it does not have a swift flight. It is said that some of these do not mate by coupling, and conceive and give birth without union; and their young live nearly to a hundred years. Vultures, like eagles, sense corpses even across the sea; for flying at a great height, they see from on high many things hidden by the darkness of the mountains. The 'gradipes' is called by the Greeks a bird that among us is slow, because, held back by its heavy flight, it is by no means lifted up with the speed of wing that other birds have. Cranes (grues) took their name from their own cry; for so they murmur in that sound. When they hasten along, they follow one another in the order of a letter-shape. Of which Lucan says: 'and the scattered letter perishes as their wings are dispersed.' They seek the heights, so as more easily to see the lands they are making for. The one whose cry drives the flock forward is called to order; and when it grows hoarse, another takes its place; by night they divide the watch and take turns keeping guard, holding pebbles in raised claws, by which they detect if they fall asleep -- for a cry gives warning of what must be guarded against. Their age is betrayed by their color; for in old age they grow black. Storks (ciconiae) are named from the sound with which they clatter, as though 'cicaniae' -- a sound made rather by the beak than by the voice, since they make it by clacking their bill. These are heralds of spring, companions in fellowship, enemies of serpents; they fly across the seas, journeying to Asia in a gathered flock. Crows lead them as guides, and follow them as though an army. They show remarkable devotion toward their young; for they cherish their nests with such diligent brooding that they shed their feathers from continual sitting. However much time they spend rearing their young, they themselves are afterward fed in turn by their own offspring for the same length of time. The swan (olor) is a bird the Greeks call kyknon. It is called olor because it is entirely white in feather -- for no one recalls a black swan; for olon in Greek means 'whole.' The cygnus (swan) is named from singing (canendo), because it pours out the sweetness of song in modulated voices. It sings so sweetly because it has a long, curved neck, and the voice, struggling through a long and winding passage, must necessarily produce varied modulations. It is said that in the Hyperborean regions, when lyre-players sing before them, a great many swans fly up and sing along most fittingly. Olores is the Latin name; for in Greek they are called kyknoi. Sailors say this bird gives them a good omen, as Aemilius says: 'the swan, among omens, is ever the happiest bird; sailors wish for it, because it does not plunge beneath the waves.' The ostrich (struthio) is called by a Greek name, because this creature seems to have the feathers of a bird in appearance, yet is never lifted higher from the ground. It neglects to brood its eggs, but merely leaving them buried, they are quickened by the warmth of the sand. The heron (ardea) is named as though ardua (lofty), that is, because of its high flight. Lucan: 'and the heron, which dares to fly.' It dreads rain, and flies above the clouds, so as not to feel the storms of the clouds. When it has flown very high, it signifies a coming storm. Many call this bird the 'Tantalus.' The phoenix is a bird of Arabia, named because it has a purple-red (phoeniceus) color, or because it is unique and singular in the whole world -- for the Arabs call something singular 'phoenix.' Living beyond five hundred years, when it sees that it has grown old, it gathers twigs of spices, builds itself a funeral pyre, and, turning to the sun's ray, nourishes with the beating of its wings a fire of its own willing, and so rises again from its own ashes. The cinnamon-bird (cinnamolgus), also of Arabia, is so named because it weaves its nests in the high woods out of the twigs of the cinnamon tree; and since men cannot climb up there because of the height and fragility of the branches, they aim leaded javelins at these same nests, and so bring down the cinnamon, and sell it for a higher price, because merchants value cinnamon more than other goods. The parrot (psittacus) is born on the shores of India, green in color, with a purple-red collar, a large tongue, broader than that of other birds. Hence it forms articulate words, so that if you did not see it, you would think it was a man speaking. By nature it greets people saying 'have' (hail), or chaire in Greek. It learns other words by training. Hence the line: 'from you, parrot, I shall learn the names of others; this I have learned to say on my own: Caesar, hail.' The kingfisher (alcyon) is a bird of the deep sea, so named as though 'ales oceanea' (ocean bird), because in winter it builds its nest and raises its young on the pools of the ocean; and while it broods, it is said that the sea, its surface stretched wide, grows mild in a continual calm of seven days, the winds falling silent, and that nature herself lends her service to the rearing of its young. The pelican is a bird of Egypt, dwelling in the wilderness of the river Nile, whence it takes its name -- for Egypt is called Canopus. It is said, if it is true, that it kills its own young, and mourns them for three days, and then wounds itself and revives its offspring by the sprinkling of its own blood. The Stymphalian birds are named from the Stymphalian islands, where they abound most; Hercules used arrows against them. They are sea-birds dwelling on the islands. The Diomedian birds are named from the companions of Diomedes, who, the legends say, were changed into these very birds; in shape like coots, in size like swans, white in color, with hard and large beaks. They dwell around Apulia, on the island of Diomedia, flying among the reefs and rocks of the shore; they judge between their own kind and strangers. For if a man is Greek, they draw near and fawn upon him; if a foreigner, they attack and wound him with their beaks, mourning, as though with tearful cries, either their own transformation or the death of their king -- for Diomedes was killed by the Illyrians. These birds are called in Latin Diomediae, the Greeks call them 'erodioi.' The Memnonian birds are named from Egypt, from the place where Memnon died. For they are said to fly in flocks from Egypt to Ilium, near the tomb of Memnon, and for this reason the people of Ilium call them Memnonian. In the fifth year they come to Ilium, and after circling for two days, on the third day, joining battle, they tear one another apart with claws and beaks in turn. The Hercynian birds are named from the Hercynian forest of Germany, where they are born, whose feathers gleam so brightly in the darkness that, however densely the night is covered in shadow, cast before the traveler they shine as a guide, and the course of the way lies open by the sign of the gleaming feathers. The Greeks call the pelican onocrotalon, from its long beak. There are two kinds: one aquatic, the other of the wilderness. The ibis is a bird of the river Nile, which purges itself, pouring water into its own anus with its beak. It feeds on the eggs of serpents, carrying this most welcome food to its nests. The bee-eaters, also called 'gauli,' are said to bury and feed their aged parents. The 'coredulus' is a kind of flying creature, as though 'heart-eating.' The jackdaw (monedula) is as though 'monetula' (little coin-bird), because when it finds gold, it carries it off and hides it. Cicero, for Valerius Flaccus: 'no more gold should be entrusted to you than to a jackdaw.' The bat (vespertilio) takes its name from the time of day, because, fleeing the light, it flies about at evening twilight, driven by a headlong motion, suspended on the very slender membranes of its arms; an animal like a mouse, resounding not so much with a voice as with a screech; it has the appearance, too, of being both a flying and a four-footed creature at once, which is not usually found in other birds. The nightingale (luscinia) took its name from this, that it is accustomed to announce with its song the rising of the coming dawn, as though 'lucinia.' It is also called 'acredula,' of which Cicero writes in his Prognostics: 'and the acredula practices its morning songs.' The screech-owl (ulula) is named apo tou ololyzein, that is, from wailing and mourning; for when it cries, it imitates either weeping or groaning. Whence, among the augurs, if it wails it is said to show sadness, but if it is silent, prosperity. The horned owl (bubo) has a name composed from the sound of its cry, a bird of ill omen, indeed heavily feathered, but always held back by a grave sluggishness; it dwells in tombs by day and night, and always lingers in caverns. Of which Ovid says: 'and it becomes a foul bird, herald of coming grief, the sluggish horned owl, a dire omen for mortals.' Indeed among the augurs it is said to portend evil: for when it is seen in a city, they say it signifies desolation. The little owl (noctua) is so called because it flies about at night and cannot see by day; for once the sun's brightness has risen, its sight grows dull. The island of Crete does not have this bird; and if it comes from elsewhere, it dies at once. The noctua is not the bubo; for the bubo is larger. The night-raven (nycticorax) is itself the noctua, because it loves the night. For it is a light-fleeing bird, and cannot bear to see the sun. The strix is a nocturnal bird, having its name from the sound of its cry; for when it cries, it screeches (stridet). Of which Lucan says: 'what the fearful horned owl, what the nocturnal strix laments.' This bird is commonly called 'amma,' from loving (amando) little ones; whence it is also said to give milk to newborns. The raven (corvus), or 'corax,' has its name from the sound of its throat, because it croaks (coracinet) with its voice. It is said that this bird does not give full food to its newly hatched young until it recognizes, by the blackening of their feathers, a likeness to its own color; but once it has seen them grown dark with feathers, having recognized them fully, it feeds them more abundantly. This bird is first to seek out the eye in a corpse. The crow (cornix), a bird of long life, is called among the Latins by a Greek name; the augurs say it directs the cares of men by its signs, shows the paths of ambushes, foretells the future. It is a great impiety to believe that God entrusts his counsels to crows. Among its many omens they attribute to it also the foretelling of rain by its cries; whence the line: 'then the wicked crow with full voice calls for rain.' The jackdaw (graculus) is named from its chattering (garrulitas), not, as some would have it, because they fly in flocks (gregatim); since it is clear they are named from their voice. For it is a very talkative kind, tiresome with its cries. Magpies (picae) are as though 'poeticae' (poetic), because they express words with a distinct articulation of voice, like man. For hanging among the branches of trees, sounding with tiresome chatter, even if they cannot form words with a tongue in speech, they nonetheless imitate the sound of a human voice...

Of which someone fittingly says: 'Chattering magpie, with a sure voice I greet you as my master: if you did not see me, you would deny that I am a bird.' The woodpecker (picus) took its name from Picus, son of Saturn, because he used this bird in taking auspices. For they say this bird has something divine about it, by this token: that in whatever tree it builds its nest, a nail, or whatever else is fixed there, cannot long remain fast without at once falling out, wherever the bird has perched. This is the woodpecker of Mars; for the pica (magpie) is another bird. The peacock (pavo) has its name from the sound of its cry; its flesh is so tough that it scarcely feels decay, nor is it easily cooked. Of which someone says: 'You marvel, whenever it spreads its jeweled wings, if you can hand this bird over to a cruel cook.' The pheasant (phasianus) is named from Phasis, an island of Greece, whence it was first brought. This is attested by the old couplet: 'First I was carried by an Argive ship: before that I knew nothing but the Phasis.' The rooster (gallus) is named from castration; for among the other birds, this alone has its testicles removed. The ancients called castrated men 'galli.' Just as leaena comes from leo, and dracaena from draco, so gallina (hen) comes from gallus. Its limbs, some say, are consumed if mixed with molten gold. The duck (anas) received its fitting name from its constant swimming (assiduitate natandi). Of this kind, certain ones are called 'germanae,' because they nurture more than the rest. The name anas gave rise to anser (goose), by derivation, or from resemblance, or because the goose too has the habit of frequent swimming. This bird keeps watch through the night with continual honking. No animal senses the smell of man as well as the goose; whence by its honking the ascent of the Gauls onto the Capitol was detected. The coot (fuliga) is so named because its flesh tastes like hare's -- for lagos is Greek for hare, whence it is also called lagos among the Greeks. It is a bird of the marshes, having its nest in the middle of the water, or on rocks surrounded by water, and always delighting in the depths of the sea. When it senses a coming storm, it flees and plays in the shallows. Divers (mergi) get their name from their constant diving (mergendi). Often, with their heads plunged into the depths, they gather signs of the winds beneath the waves, and, foreseeing a storm at sea, head for the shore with loud cries. For a storm at sea is already known to be very severe when the divers take refuge on the shore. The hawk (accipiter) is a bird armed more in spirit than in talons, bearing greater strength in a smaller body. It takes its name from accipiendo, that is, from seizing (capiendo). For it is a bird eager to seize other birds, and so is called accipiter, that is, 'seizer.' Whence the Apostle Paul says: 'For you suffer, if a man seize (accipit) you.' As if to say 'if he seizes,' he said 'if he takes.' It is said that hawks are unkind toward their young; for once they see they are able to attempt flight, they give them no more food, but beat them with their wings and cast them from the nest, and drive them from their tender youth toward hunting, lest, once grown, they become lazy. The 'capus,' in the Italian tongue, is named from capiendo (seizing). Our people call this the falcon, because its talons are curved (falx). The kite (milvus) is weak both in strength and in flight, as though 'mollis avis' (soft bird), whence its name; yet it is most rapacious, and always lies in ambush for domestic birds. The osprey (ossifragus) is commonly called the bird that drops bones from a height and breaks them; whence it takes its name from 'breaking bones' (ossa frangendo). The turtledove (turtur) is named from its call; a modest bird, always dwelling on mountain ridges and in the solitudes of the wilderness. For it avoids the roofs and company of men, and dwells in the woods...

div.head: On the Smaller Flying Creatures
div.p: Bees (apes) are so named either because they bind themselves together by their feet, or because they are born without feet -- for afterward they receive both feet and wings. These skillful creatures inhabit dwellings assigned to the task of producing honey, build homes of indescribable craft, gather honeycomb from various flowers, and with their woven wax fill their encampments with countless offspring; they have an army and kings, they wage battles, they flee smoke, and are provoked by uproar. Many have observed that these are born from the carcasses of oxen. For to bring these into being, the flesh of slaughtered calves is beaten, so that from the putrefied blood worms are created, which afterward become bees. Properly, however, bees are said to arise from oxen, just as hornets arise from horses, drone-bees from mules, wasps from donkeys. The Greeks call the larger bees, born at the outer edges of the combs, 'kestroi'; some think these are the kings. They are so named because they lead the camp (castra ducant). The drone (fugus) is larger than the bee, smaller than the hornet. It is named fugus because it eats the labor of others, as though fagus; for it feeds on what it has not labored for. Of which Virgil says: 'the lazy drones they drive from the hives.' Wasps. Hornets (scabrones) are named from cabo, that is, from caballus (horse), because they are born from them. And just as hornets are born from the putrid flesh of horses, so from these in turn are often born beetles (scarabaei), whence they take their name. Bulls (tauri) is the name given to earthly beetles resembling the tick. The buprestis is a small creature in Italy, most like a beetle, with long legs. It deceives the ox chiefly among the grasses, whence it takes its name, and once swallowed, touching the gall, inflames it so that it bursts. The firefly (cicindela) is a kind of beetle, so named because, walking or flying, it gives light. Cockroaches (blattae) are named from their color, since when caught they also stain the hand; whence too the color 'blatteus' is named. This creature cannot bear to see light -- the opposite of the fly, for the fly seeks the light, while the cockroach flees it; for it walks about only by night. Butterflies (papiliones) are little winged creatures that abound especially where mallows flower, and which cause little worms to be born from their own droppings. The locust (locusta) is named because it has long feet, like a spear (hasta); whence the Greeks call both the sea-locust and the land-locust 'astakos.' Cicadas are born from the spittle of cuckoos. In Italy, among the Rhegians, these are mute, and nowhere else. The fly (musca) comes from the Greek, as does 'mus' (mouse). This creature, like the bee, when killed in water, sometimes revives after the space of an hour. The Greeks call it 'cynomya,' that is, dog-fly; for kyon in Greek means dog. The gnat (culex) is named from its sting (aculeus), because it sucks blood. For it has in its mouth a tube like a goad, with which it bores the flesh to drink blood. The 'sciniphes' are very tiny flies, extremely troublesome with their stings. By this third plague the proud people of the Egyptians were struck down. The gadfly (oestrus) is a creature that torments herds of cattle, very troublesome with its stings. Oestrus is a Greek word, called in Latin asilus, commonly tabanus. The 'bibiones' are creatures born in wine, commonly called 'mustiones,' from must (new wine). Whence Afranius says: 'when you look at me and begin to speak, gnats fly from your mouth into your eyes.' The 'gurgulio' (weevil) is so named because it is almost nothing but a throat (guttur).
